explanations.explanation: Malta it is, baker. Acts 28:1 says that once they were safely ashore, they learned the island was called Malta. Nobody on that beach had to guess. After a shipwreck, I bet a name on the map felt like a warm blanket.

Crete is a real island in this voyage, but it's not where they land. Acts 28:1 says they learned the island was called Malta. I think after a shipwreck, nobody was in the mood for a geography quiz, and they just wanted a name to go with the dry sand.

Cyprus is another island you'll hear about in Acts, but this isn't it. Acts 28:1 says that once they were safely ashore, they learned the island was called Malta. That's the name to remember for this stop.

explanations.answer: They kindle a fire and welcome them all
explanations.explanation: That's the one. Acts 28:2 says the islanders "kindled a fire and welcomed all of us because it was raining and cold." A fire for a soaked crowd of strangers is about the best welcome I can think of. And they welcomed ALL of them, no picking and choosing.

explanations.answer: They lead them all to shelter in a cave
explanations.explanation: A cave sounds cozy, but the text never mentions one. Acts 28:2 says the islanders "kindled a fire and welcomed all of us because it was raining and cold." The fire was the kindness, and I think a roaring fire beats any cave on a wet, cold day.

explanations.answer: They hand out dry cloaks to everyone
explanations.explanation: Dry cloaks would've been lovely, friend, but the text doesn't say that. Acts 28:2 says the islanders "kindled a fire and welcomed all of us because it was raining and cold." A fire dries the cloaks AND warms the people inside them.

A viper, baker. Acts 28:3 says it was "driven out by the heat" and fastened itself to Paul's hand as he laid sticks on the fire. That snake was minding its own business in that bundle, and Paul never saw it coming. I'd have launched that bundle into the sea.

Close in spirit, but a scorpion isn't what the text says. Acts 28:3 says a viper, "driven out by the heat," fastened itself to Paul's hand as he laid sticks on the fire. Paul just wanted to help with the fire, and the fire sent the viper right to him.

A lizard would've made this a much calmer story, friend. But Acts 28:3 says a viper, "driven out by the heat," fastened itself to Paul's hand. That's why the islanders started talking in the next verse.

Yes, a murderer. In Acts 28:4 the islanders say to one another, "Surely this man is a murderer. Although he was saved from the sea, Justice has not allowed him to live." They jumped to a big conclusion in about two seconds. I think we've all been quick to judge a situation we only half saw.

Not a sorcerer, baker. Acts 28:4 has the islanders saying, "Surely this man is a murderer." They said it because of the creature hanging from his hand, and they added that Justice had not allowed him to live.

That's not what they said. In Acts 28:4 the islanders say, "Surely this man is a murderer. Although he was saved from the sea, Justice has not allowed him to live." Murderer was the word, and it was a heavy thing to say about a man who'd just come out of a shipwreck.
Not quite. Acts 28:5 says Paul shook the creature off into the fire and "suffered no ill effects." No swelling, no collapse, nothing. The viper got a hot ending, and Paul got on with his day.

False is right. Acts 28:5 says Paul shook the creature off into the fire and "suffered no ill effects." He just shook it off, like a man brushing crumbs off his apron. The islanders were about to be very confused.

True. Acts 28:6 says that after waiting a long time and seeing nothing unusual happen to him, the islanders changed their minds and said he was a god. They had a whole new opinion after watching a little longer. I'd have loved to hear that group chat.

It's actually true, friend. Acts 28:6 says that after waiting a long time and seeing nothing unusual happen to Paul, the islanders changed their minds and said he was a god. They'd been expecting him to swell up or suddenly drop dead, and when that never came, they flipped completely.

explanations.answer: He welcomes and hosts them for three days
explanations.explanation: That's the one. Acts 28:7 says Publius "welcomed us and entertained us hospitably for three days." Publius was the chief official of the island, and he opened up his estate to a bunch of shipwrecked strangers. That's a lot of guests for one house.

explanations.answer: He has them held under guard
explanations.explanation: No guards in this scene. Acts 28:7 says Publius, the chief official, "welcomed us and entertained us hospitably for three days." Hospitably is the word. Hosting beats holding, every time.

explanations.answer: He orders them off his estate
explanations.explanation: The opposite happened, baker. Acts 28:7 says Publius "welcomed us and entertained us hospitably for three days." He was the chief official of the island, and he opened his door instead of closing it.

explanations.answer: He prays and places his hands on him
explanations.explanation: Right. Acts 28:8 says Paul went in to see him, and "after praying and placing his hands on him, he healed the man." Paul prayed first, and the man was healed. The father of Publius had been in bed with fever and dysentery.

explanations.answer: He anoints him with oil and leaves
explanations.explanation: That's not what the text says, friend. Acts 28:8 says Paul went in to see him, and "after praying and placing his hands on him, he healed the man." No oil is mentioned, and Paul didn't leave a sick man in bed. He went in and prayed.

explanations.answer: He sends for the island's physician
explanations.explanation: No physician in this verse. Acts 28:8 says Paul went in to see the man, and "after praying and placing his hands on him, he healed the man." Paul went right to the bedside himself.

explanations.answer: The rest of the sick on the island
explanations.explanation: Yes! Acts 28:9 says that after this happened, "the rest of the sick on the island came and were cured as well." Word got around fast on that little island. I think the line outside Publius's house got long.
The text goes much wider than that, baker. Acts 28:9 says "the rest of the sick on the island came and were cured as well." It's the whole island's sick, not just one household.

The soldiers aren't mentioned in this verse. Acts 28:9 says "the rest of the sick on the island came and were cured as well." That means the sick across the whole island, which is a much bigger crowd.

True. Acts 28:10 says the islanders "honored us in many ways and supplied our needs when we were ready to sail." Think about that. They started with a fire on a cold beach and ended by sending the travelers off with what they needed. That's kindness from start to finish.

It's true, friend. Acts 28:10 says the islanders "honored us in many ways and supplied our needs when we were ready to sail." They were kind at the start with the fire, and they were still kind at the end when it was time to leave.
